question: How do precise measurements of rare B-meson decays to muon pairs constrain theories beyond the Standard Model, and which classes of new-physics models are most strongly affected?
seed_answer:
### 1.  Why the decay \(B_q^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-\) is such a powerful probe  

| Feature | What it means for new‑physics (NP) searches |
|---------|---------------------------------------------|
| **Flavor‑changing neutral current (FCNC)** | In the SM this transition occurs only via loops (penguin & box diagrams). No tree‑level diagram exists, so the SM amplitude is tiny (CKM‑suppressed \(\sim V_{tb}V_{tq}^*\) and loop‑suppressed \(\alpha_{\rm em}/4\pi\)). |
| **Helicity suppression** | The SM amplitude is proportional to the lepton mass, \(\mathcal A_{\rm SM}\propto m_\mu\). This further reduces the branching fraction to \(\mathcal O(10^{-10})\) for \(B_s^0\) and \(\mathcal O(10^{-11})\) for \(B_d^0\). |
| **Theoretical cleanliness** | The hadronic matrix element reduces to a single decay constant \(f_{B_q}\). Lattice QCD now provides \(f_{B_s}= (230.3\pm 1.3)\,\text{MeV}\) and \(f_{B_d}= (190.0\pm 1.2)\,\text{MeV}\) with sub‑percent uncertainties. Long‑distance photon‑exchange contributions are negligible. |
| **Experimental accessibility** | The final state is fully reconstructible with excellent vertex resolution and muon identification; LHCb, CMS and ATLAS have measured the rates with \(\sim10\%\) precision. |
| **SM “null test”** | Any deviation of the measured branching fraction (or related observables: effective lifetime, CP asymmetry) from the SM prediction immediately signals NP. |

Because the SM prediction is small and theoretically precise, **even percent‑level changes** induced by NP are experimentally visible. This makes \(B_{s,d}^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-\) one of the cleanest indirect NP probes.

---

### 2.  How the measurement is translated into constraints

#### 2.1 Effective‑Hamiltonian language  

At the scale \(\mu\sim m_b\) the decay is described by the effective Hamiltonian  

\[
\mathcal H_{\rm eff}= -\frac{4G_F}{\sqrt2}\,V_{tb}V_{tq}^\ast
\sum_i C_i(\mu)\,\mathcal O_i(\mu) \; ,
\]

with the most relevant operators for the muon‑pair mode:

| Operator | SM Wilson coefficient | Typical NP entry |
|----------|-----------------------|-------------------|
| \(\mathcal O_{10}= (\bar q \gamma_\mu P_L b)(\bar\mu\gamma^\mu\gamma_5\mu)\) | \(C_{10}^{\rm SM}\simeq -4.1\) (real) | Shifted by Z‑penguin, box, leptoquark exchange etc. |
| \(\mathcal O_S = m_b (\bar q P_R b)(\bar\mu\mu)\) | Negligible (tiny scalar Higgs contribution) | Can be generated by Higgs‑mediated FCNC, leptoquarks, R‑parity‑violating SUSY |
| \(\mathcal O_P = m_b (\bar q P_R b)(\bar\mu\gamma_5\mu)\) | Negligible | Pseudoscalar exchange (e.g. pseudo‑scalar Higgs \(A^0\) in 2HDM) |
| \(\mathcal O_{10}^\prime,\mathcal O_{S}^\prime,\mathcal O_{P}^\prime\) | Zero in SM (right‑handed currents) | Appear in models with right‑handed gauge bosons or chiral leptoquarks |

The **branching fraction** (ignoring tiny CP‑violating effects) can be written compactly as  

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal B(B_q\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)=
\frac{G_F^2\alpha^2}{16\pi^3}
\,\tau_{B_q} f_{B_q}^2 M_{B_q} m_\mu^2
\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_\mu^2}{M_{B_q}^2}}
\,
\big|V_{tb}V_{tq}^\ast\big|^2
\big( |P|^2+|S|^2 \big)
}
\]

where  

\[
P = C_{10}^{\rm SM}+ C_{10}^{\rm NP} - \frac{M_{B_q}^2}{2m_\mu}\frac{C_P-C_P'}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}},\qquad
S = \frac{M_{B_q}^2}{2m_\mu}\frac{C_S-C_S'}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}} .
\]

Thus **any NP that modifies \(C_{10}\), or generates sizable scalar/pseudoscalar coefficients**, will change the rate.

#### 2.2 Using the experimental numbers  

Current world averages (LHCb + CMS + ATLAS, 2024)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B(B_s^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)&=(3.09\pm0.19)\times10^{-9},\\[2pt]
\mathcal B(B_d^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)&=(1.00\pm0.15)\times10^{-10},
\end{aligned}
\]

to be compared with the SM predictions (including N\(^3\)LO QCD and NLO EW)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B_{\rm SM}(B_s^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)&=(3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9},\\
\mathcal B_{\rm SM}(B_d^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)&=(1.06\pm0.04)\times10^{-10}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The **ratio**  

\[
R_{\mu\mu}\equiv \frac{\mathcal B(B_d\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)}{\mathcal B(B_s\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)}
 =0.032\pm0.006\qquad(\text{SM: }0.029\pm0.001)
\]

is also a clean observable because the CKM factors and decay constants largely cancel.  

From these numbers one extracts **allowed ranges** for the Wilson coefficients. For illustration (assuming NP appears only in a single coefficient and is real):

| Coefficient | 95 % CL bound (approximately) |
|-------------|-------------------------------|
| \(\Delta C_{10}\) | \([-0.5,\,0.3]\) |
| \(C_S\)              | \(|C_S| \lesssim 0.03\) |
| \(C_P\)              | \(|C_P| \lesssim 0.04\) |
| \(C_{10}^\prime\)    | \(|C_{10}^\prime| \lesssim 0.2\) |
| \(C_S^\prime\)       | \(|C_S^\prime| \lesssim 0.04\) |
| \(C_P^\prime\)       | \(|C_P^\prime| \lesssim 0.05\) |

These limits are **orders of magnitude tighter** than those obtained from other rare‑decay channels such as \(B\!\to K^{(*)}\ell^+\ell^-\) (which suffer from larger form‑factor uncertainties) or from inclusive \(b\to s\ell^+\ell^-\) measurements.

---

### 3.  Classes of new‑physics models most strongly constrained  

Below is a “road‑map” of the NP frameworks that are hit hardest by the \(\,B_{s,d}\!\to\mu^+\mu^-\) data.

| Model class | Typical mediators affecting the decay | Dominant operator(s) generated | How the data constrain the model |
|-------------|---------------------------------------|-------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Supersymmetry (SUSY) with large \(\tan\beta\)** | Heavy neutral Higgses (\(H^0, A^0\)) and (sometimes) gluino‑squark loops | Scalar & pseudoscalar operators (\(C_S, C_P\)) ∝ \(\tan^3\beta/M_A^2\) | For \(\tan\beta\gtrsim 30\) one needs \(M_A\gtrsim 1.5\text{–}2\) TeV (or small flavor‑changing squark mixings). The bound rivals direct LHC searches for heavy Higgses. |
| **Two‑Higgs‑Doublet Models (2HDM, especially Type‑II & aligned)** | Extra neutral scalars (H, A) and charged Higgs (H⁺) in loops | \(C_S, C_P\) (tree level if FCNC Yukawas allowed) and shifts in \(C_{10}\) | The current \(\mathcal B\) forces \(\frac{\tan\beta}{M_A}\lesssim (30\,\text{GeV})^{-1}\). In the “aligned” 2HDM with small alignment parameter the constraint translates to \(|\varsigma_d\varsigma_\ell|\lesssim 0.02(M_A/1\text{ TeV})^2\). |
| **Z′ bosons / extra gauge bosons** | Tree‑level flavour‑changing \(Z′\) couplings to \(\bar b\,q\) and to muons | Modification of \(C_{10}\) (and possibly \(C_{10}^\prime\)) | The bound \(|\Delta C_{10}|\lesssim0.5\) implies \(\frac{g^{\prime}_{bq}\,g^{\prime}_{\mu\mu}}{M_{Z′}^2}\lesssim (1\!-\!2)\times10^{-9}\,\text{GeV}^{-2}\). For unit couplings this pushes \(M_{Z′}\) above ≈ 5 TeV, already stronger than typical Drell‑Yan limits for flavour‑non‑universal models. |
| **Leptoquarks (LQ)** | Scalar LQ \(S_{1},\,R_{2}\) or vector LQ \(U_{1},\,U_{3}\) coupling to \(b\)-quark and muon | Both vector‑axial (\(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\)) and scalar/pseudoscalar (\(C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}\)) depending on chirality | Fits to the \(B\to K^{(*)}\mu^+\mu^-\) anomalies favour \(C_{9}^{\mu\mu}\) shifts; the same couplings also generate \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\). The \(\mu^+\mu^-\) branching ratios then restrict the product \(\lambda_{b\mu}\lambda_{s\mu}\) to be \(\lesssim 0.02\,(M_{\rm LQ}/{\rm 1\,TeV})^2\). This excludes large‑coupling LQ explanations unless the LQ is heavier than ∼2 TeV. |
| **Models with vector‑like quarks (VLQ)** | Mixing of SM \(b\) with heavy down‑type VLQs induces tree‑level FCNC Z couplings | Shift in \(C_{10}\) (mostly left‑handed) | The data force the off‑diagonal Z coupling \(|\Delta g_{L}^{bs}|\lesssim 1.5\times10^{-4}\). Translating into VLQ mass–mixing parameters gives \(M_{\rm VLQ}\gtrsim 3\) TeV for mixing angles of order \(10^{-2}\). |
| **Flavor‑changing axion‑like particles (ALPs) or light pseudoscalars** | Very light (MeV‑GeV) pseudoscalars coupling to \(\bar b s\) and to \(\mu\) | Generates an *effective* \(C_P\) proportional to \(\frac{g_{bs} g_{\mu\mu}}{m_A^2}\) | For \(m_A\ll M_{B_s}\) the bound becomes \(|g_{bs}g_{\mu\mu}| \lesssim 10^{-9}\). This is comparable to limits from \(B\to K\ell^+\ell^-\) but more stringent because of the helicity suppression removal. |
| **Composite Higgs / partial‑compositeness** | Heavy spin‑1 resonances (\(\rho\)) and fermionic top partners that couple to left-handed currents | Mainly \(C_{10}\) and right‑handed \(C_{10}^\prime\) | The combined LHCb‑CMS result pushes compositeness scales to \(f\gtrsim 1.5\) TeV for typical coupling strengths (\(g_\rho\sim3\)). |

> **Bottom line:**  The strongest impact is on *scalar/pseudoscalar* operators (because they lift the SM helicity suppression) and on *vector/axial* operators that modify the Z‑penguin.  Models that predict large \(\tan\beta\)‑enhanced Higgs exchange, tree‑level flavour‑changing Z′ or leptoquark couplings, or sizable mixing of SM quarks with heavy vector‑like states are therefore the ones most tightly squeezed.

---

### 4.  Complementary observables that sharpen the picture  

| Observable | What it adds | Current status |
|------------|--------------|----------------|
| **Effective lifetime \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) of \(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-\)** | Sensitive to the relative size of \(P\) vs. \(S\) because the heavy‑light eigenstate mixture changes the decay‑time distribution. | Measured by LHCb: \(\tau_{\mu\mu}=2.07\pm0.13\) ps, consistent with SM (which predicts \(\approx 1.61\) ps for pure \(P\)). Large scalar contributions would push \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) toward the heavy‑state lifetime (\(\sim1.61\) ps). |
| **CP asymmetry \(\mathcal A_{\Delta\Gamma}\)** | Direct probe of the CP‑violating phase of \(P\) or \(S\). | Not yet measured precisely; future Run‑3+HL‑LHC will reach \(\sim10\%\) precision, enough to test models with new CP phases (e.g. complex Yukawas in 2HDM). |
| **\(B\to K^{(*)}\mu^+\mu^-\) angular observables (\(P_5'\), \(R_K\), \(R_{K^*}\))** | Constrain the same operators \(C_{9,10}^{(\prime)}\) but with larger hadronic uncertainties. | Show persistent tensions (≈ 3 σ) that favour a negative shift in \(C_9^\mu\). Consistency with \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^+\mu^-\) forces NP to be predominantly in left‑handed vector currents, not scalar ones. |
| **\(B\to\mu\nu\) and \(B\to D^{(*)}\tau\nu\)** | Test charged‑Higgs contributions related to the same \(\tan\beta/M_A\) parameter entering scalar operators. | Current bounds are compatible, but the combined global fit tightens the allowed \(\tan\beta\)–\(M_A\) plane. |
| **Direct searches for heavy mediators (Z′, H/A, LQ)** | Provide independent mass limits that can be combined with the indirect bounds. | LHC excludes \(M_{Z′}\lesssim 4\)–5 TeV (depending on couplings) and \(M_{H/A}\lesssim 1\) TeV for large \(\tan\beta\). The indirect bounds from \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^+\mu^-\) are comparable or even stronger for the same coupling choices. |

---

### 5.  Outlook – how the constraints will improve

| Future milestone | Expected experimental precision | Impact on NP limits |
|-------------------|----------------------------------|---------------------|
| **LHCb Upgrade I (Run 3, 2029)** | \(\delta\mathcal B(B_s\to\mu\mu) \sim 5\%\), \(\delta\tau_{\mu\mu}\sim 5\%\) | Scalar coefficients probed at the \(\sim10^{-3}\) level, closing the window on moderate‑\(\tan\beta\) SUSY. |
| **HL‑LHC combined ATLAS+CMS+LHCb (≈300 fb\(^{-1}\))** | \(\sim 3\%\) on both \(B_s\) and \(B_d\) rates | Ratio \(R_{\mu\mu}\) reaches 2 % accuracy → tests MFV‑type relations and can reveal tiny right‑handed currents. |
| **FCC‑eh / CEPC / Belle II (high‑luminosity e⁺e⁻)** | Belle II may reach \(\sim 15\%\) on \(B_d\to\mu\mu\) (complementary environment) | Provides cross‑check of systematic effects and adds sensitivity to possible lepton‑flavour‑non‑universality (e.g. \(B\to e^+e^-\) vs. \(\mu^+\mu^-\)). |
| **Theory: lattice QCD** | Decay constants to \(\lesssim0.3\%\) (target) | Reduces the SM error below the experimental one, turning the mode into a *precision* SM test rather than a purely NP discovery channel. |

When experimental uncertainties shrink below the **few‑percent** level, the constraints on the Wilson coefficients will tighten by roughly a factor of two. This will push many NP scales beyond 10 TeV (for order‑one couplings) or force couplings to be \(\lesssim10^{-2}\) for TeV‑scale mediators.

---

## 6.  TL;DR Summary

* **Rare decays \(B_{s,d}^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-\)** are loop‑ and helicity‑suppressed in the SM, leading to tiny, precisely predicted branching fractions.
* The measured rates agree with the SM within \(\sim5\%\), which translates into **tight bounds on the effective Wilson coefficients** \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) (vector/axial) and especially on **scalar/pseudoscalar coefficients** \(C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}\) that would lift the helicity suppression.
* Consequently, any NP model that induces:
  * **Tree‑level flavour‑changing neutral currents** (Z′, leptoquarks, vector‑like quarks),
  * **Enhanced Higgs‑mediated scalar currents** (large‑\(\tan\beta\) SUSY, 2HDM),
  * **New CP‑violating phases** in the \(b\to s\) sector,
  is forced into a **high‑mass / small‑coupling regime** (typically \(M \gtrsim 2\)–5 TeV for order‑one couplings).
* The **most strongly affected classes** are: high‑\(\tan\beta\) supersymmetry, generic two‑Higgs‑doublet models, flavour‑non‑universal Z′ models, and leptoquark scenarios that also aim to explain the \(b\to s\ell\ell\) anomalies.
* Future LHCb upgrades, the HL‑LHC, and improved lattice inputs will sharpen these constraints, turning \(B_{s,d}\!\to\mu^+\mu^-\) into a **precision probe of new physics at scales well beyond the direct reach of colliders**.

question: What are the key best practices and evaluation criteria for validating synthetic medical images generated by GANs so they can be trusted and safely used in clinical workflows?
seed_answer:
Below is a **practical, step‑by‑step framework** that you can use to **validate synthetic medical images generated by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)** and to decide whether they are trustworthy enough to be used—​even in regulated clinical workflows. The framework is organized into three layers: | Layer | Goal | Key Practices | Core Evaluation Metrics | |-------|------|----------------|--------------------------| | **1️⃣ Technical Fidelity** | Prove that the synthetic images are *indistinguishable* from real ones in terms of low‑level image statistics and anatomy. | • Pixel‑level similarity checks
• Distribution‑level comparison
• Artefact detection
• Multi‑modal consistency (e.g., CT ↔︎ MRI) | • PSNR, SSIM, MS‑SSIM
• Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) – adapted to medical feature extractors
• Kernel Inception Distance (KID)
• Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS)
• Wasserstein distance on radiomics feature vectors | | **2️⃣ Clinical Validity** | Show that the images preserve *diagnostically relevant* information and do not bias downstream tasks. | • Expert radiologist / pathologist blind review
• Down‑stream task performance (segmentation, detection, classification)
• Clinical utility tests (e.g., reader studies, ROC analysis)
• Task‑specific invariance testing (e.g., lesion size, contrast) | • Sensitivity / Specificity, AUROC, F1 on downstream AI models
• Kappa (inter‑rater agreement) between real vs. synthetic reads
• Mean Absolute Error (MAE) on quantitative biomarkers (e.g., tumor volume, Hounsfield Units)
• “Clinical fidelity score” – a composite of reader confidence, lesion detectability, and diagnostic accuracy | | **3️⃣ Regulatory & Ethical Assurance** | Meet privacy, bias, reproducibility, and safety requirements required by health‑technology regulators (FDA, EMA, MHRA, etc.). | • Privacy audit (membership inference, model inversion)
• Bias analysis across demographics & acquisition sites
• Version control & provenance tracking
• Stress testing under domain shift (different scanners, protocols)
• Documentation & Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for generation & use | • Differential privacy ε‑budget (if applied)
• Statistical parity / equalized odds across sub‑groups
• Failure‑mode rate under controlled perturbations
• Reproducibility score (e.g., % identical output for same seed + hardware)
• Compliance checklist (FDA’s “Software as a Medical Device” (SaMD) guidance, ISO/IEC 14971 risk management) | Below each layer is expanded with **actionable best‑practice checklists**, **why the metric matters**, and **how to present the evidence** when seeking regulatory clearance or institutional adoption. --- ## 1️⃣ Technical Fidelity – “Does it look real?” ### 1.1. Data‑level preprocessing sanity‑check | ✔️ Action | Why | |---|---| | **Standardize intensity & spacing** (e.g., HU normalization for CT, z‑score for MRI) before feeding both real & synthetic images into any metric. | Guarantees that measured differences are due to content, not scaling artifacts. | | **Match acquisition metadata** (slice thickness, reconstruction kernel, field‑of‑view). | Prevents the metric from penalizing legitimate protocol differences. | ### 1.2. Low‑level similarity metrics | Metric | How to compute (medical‑specific tip) | Acceptable range (rule‑of‑thumb) | |---|---|---| | **Peak Signal‑to‑Noise Ratio (PSNR)** | Compute on paired real‑synthetic images if a *conditional* GAN is used. Use a small ROI where anatomy is stable (e.g., brain white matter). | > 30 dB for CT, > 28 dB for MRI is typically “high‑quality”. | | **Structural Similarity Index (SSIM / MS‑SSIM)** | Operate on 3‑D patches (e.g., 32³ voxels). Weight luminance, contrast, structure equally. | > 0.95 for brain MRI, > 0.90 for abdominal CT. | | **LPIPS (Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity)** | Use a network pre‑trained on medical data (e.g., Med3D, RadImageNet) as the feature extractor. | < 0.15 (lower = more perceptually similar). | | **Radiomics distribution comparison** | Extract 100+ radiomic features (first‑order, texture, shape) from both sets; compare with Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test or Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD). | p‑value > 0.05 for KS (no statistically significant difference). | ### 1.3. Distribution‑level metrics | Metric | How to compute | Rationale | |---|---|---| | **Fréchet Inception Distance (FID)** | Replace the generic Inception‑v3 embedding with a domain‑specific encoder (e.g., a ResNet‑50 trained on ChestX‑Ray14). Compute mean & covariance on embeddings from a large pool (≥ 5 000 samples). | Captures higher‑order statistics of the whole dataset, not just pixel‑wise similarity. | | **Kernel Inception Distance (KID)** | Same as FID but uses a polynomial kernel; unbiased estimator. | More stable with smaller sample sizes (≈ 1 000). | | **Precision‑Recall for Generative Models** | Estimate *precision* (how many synthetic samples fall within the support of real data) and *recall* (coverage of real distribution). Use the *k‑nearest neighbour* method in embedding space. | Directly measures mode collapse (low recall) and hallucination (low precision). | | **t‑SNE / UMAP visual inspection** | Project embeddings of real & synthetic sets onto 2‑D; look for overlap. | Quick sanity check for distributional drift. | ### 1.4. Artefact & Failure‑Mode detection | Test | Procedure | Pass criteria | |---|---|---| | **Synthetic‑only artefact audit** | Run a pretrained segmentation model (e.g., lung nodule detector) on synthetic images; flag cases where the model predicts impossible shapes or out‑of‑range intensities. | ≤ 1 % of synthetic images flagged. | | **Histogram & contrast consistency** | Compare intensity histograms per organ/ tissue class. Compute Jensen‑Shannon divergence. | JSD < 0.02. | | **Spatial consistency** | For conditional GANs that take a label map as input, compute Dice between input mask and mask extracted from the generated image (e.g., using a pre‑trained organ segmentation network). | Dice > 0.95. | --- ## 2️⃣ Clinical Validity – “Does it preserve what matters for diagnosis?” ### 2.1. Expert blind‑review study | Step | Details | |---|---| | **Sample selection** | Randomly sample 200–500 real and synthetic cases, balanced across disease severity and acquisition sites. | | **Blinding** | Remove all DICOM tags that could betray origin; present images in mixed order. | | **Readout** | Ask ≥ 3 experienced radiologists (or pathologists) to rate:
1. *Real vs. Synthetic* (binary).
2. *Diagnostic confidence* (1‑5 Likert).
3. *Presence/absence of target lesion*. | | **Metrics** | • **AUC for real vs. synthetic classification** – should be ≈ 0.5 (chance).
• **Inter‑rater agreement (Cohen’s κ)** – should be comparable between real and synthetic groups.
• **Mean confidence score** – no statistically significant drop (p > 0.05). | | **Reporting** | Provide a CONSORT‑style flow diagram, confidence intervals, and a *non‑inferiority* statistical test (e.g., Δ ≤ 0.05). | ### 2‑3. Down‑stream task performance | Task | Typical benchmark | Acceptance criterion | |---|---|---| | **Segmentation (e.g., liver, tumor)** | Train model on *real + synthetic* vs. *real‑only*. Report Dice, IoU, Hausdorff. | ΔDice ≥ +0.02 (synthetic improves) **or** ΔDice ≤ −0.01 (synthetic does not degrade). | | **Classification (e.g., COVID‑19 vs. normal)** | Compare AUROC, sensitivity at fixed specificity. | Non‑inferiority margin of 0.03 AUROC. | | **Detection (e.g., pulmonary nodule)** | Free‑response ROC (FROC) curves; compute sensitivity at 1 FP/scan. | ≤ 2 % loss compared with real‑only training. | | **Quantitative biomarkers** (e.g., tumor volume, bone mineral density) | Compute MAE/percent error vs. ground truth. | MAE < 5 % of clinical tolerance. | ### 2‑4. Clinical utility / reader‑study augmentation | Design | Outcome | |---|---| | **Real‑only vs. Real + Synthetic augmentation** | Show that adding synthetic data reduces the number of cases needed to reach a target performance (power analysis). | | **Synthetic as “training‑set expansion”** | Demonstrate that models trained on a *smaller* real dataset + synthetic reach the same performance as a *larger* pure real dataset (cost‑benefit). | ### 2‑5. Task‑specific invariance checks | Invariance | Test | |---|---| | **Lesion size** | Plot model output vs. ground‑truth lesion diameter for real vs. synthetic; slope ≈ 1, R² > 0.9. | | **Contrast variation** | Vary synthetic contrast levels (e.g., simulate different injection phases) and ensure downstream model performance is stable (ΔAUROC < 0.02). | | **Anatomical pose** | Rotate or flip synthetic images and verify that the model’s predictions are equivariant (within 1 % tolerance). | --- ## 3️⃣ Regulatory & Ethical Assurance – “Is it safe, fair, and auditable?” ### 3‑1. Privacy guarantees | Technique | Check | |---|---| | **Membership inference attacks** | Attempt to recover whether a specific patient appears in the training set using state‑of‑the‑art attack (e.g., shadow models). Success rate ≤ 55 % (close to random). | | **Model inversion** | Reconstruct a plausible patient image from the generator’s latent space; visual inspection must not reveal identifiable anatomy. | | **Differential privacy (DP‑GAN)** | If DP is used, report ε budget (e.g., ε ≤ 5) and demonstrate that utility loss stays within the clinical thresholds defined above. | ### 3‑2. Bias & fairness analysis | Dimension | Method | |---|---| | **Demographics (age, sex, ethnicity)** | Stratify synthetic set by these variables (if conditional generation is used). Compare prevalence and radiomic distributions with real data (Chi‑square, KS). | | **Scanner/vendor** | Generate synthetic images conditioned on vendor; verify that downstream model performance is invariant across vendors (ANOVA, post‑hoc Tukey). | | **Disease severity** | Ensure that rare severe cases are not under‑represented (e.g., check class‑wise FID). | ### 3‑3. Robustness & domain‑shift testing | Scenario | Procedure | |---|---| | **Out‑of‑distribution scanners** | Apply the generator to images from a scanner not seen during training; run the same technical & clinical metrics. | | **Noise & motion simulation** | Add realistic noise, motion blur, or low‑dose artifacts to synthetic images; confirm that they still pass quality thresholds. | | **Adversarial perturbations** | Apply small (‖δ‖₂ < 0.01) adversarial noise to latent vectors; verify that generated images do not collapse into “noise mode”. | ### 3‑4. Documentation, Traceability & Versioning | Requirement | How to satisfy | |---|---| | **Model provenance** | Store Git commit hash, training dataset snapshot (hash), hyper‑parameters, random seed, Docker image ID. | | **Dataset lineage** | Keep a *data‑sheet* for the real dataset (source, consent, de‑identification steps). | | **Change‑control log** | Every model update must be accompanied by a “validation report” that repeats the full suite of metrics above. | | **Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)** | Define who can trigger generation, review steps, storage location (e.g., PACS with `Synthetic` tag), and expiration policy (e.g., regenerate every 12 months). | ### 3‑5. Regulatory pathways | Agency | Relevant guidance | Typical submission artefacts | |---|---|---| | **FDA (US)** | *Software as a Medical Device (SaMD)*, *Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP)*, *Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) Software‑as‑Medical‑Device Action Plan* | • Technical Validation Dossier (metrics above)
• Clinical Validation Dossier (reader studies)
• Risk Management File (ISO 14971) | | **EMA (EU)** | *MDR 2017/745* Annex I, *EU AI Act* (if classified as high‑risk) | Same as FDA plus CE‑mark technical documentation. | | **MHRA (UK)** | *UK MDR 2002* (post‑Brexit) | Emphasis on post‑market surveillance plan for synthetic data pipelines. | | **Health Canada** | *Medical Device Regulations (SOR/98‑282)* | Similar to FDA, with additional privacy impact assessment. | *Tip*: Draft a **“Synthetic Data Validation Summary (SDVS)”** that lists every metric, its target, observed value, and a pass/fail flag. This one‑page table is what regulators love to see. --- ## QUICK‑START CHECKLIST (One‑Page) | ✅ Category | ✔️ Must‑Do | 📏 Target / Pass | |---|---|---| | **Pixel fidelity** | PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS on paired samples (if conditional). | PSNR > 30 dB, SSIM > 0.95, LPIPS < 0.15 | | **Distribution fidelity** | FID/KID with medical encoder; Precision‑Recall. | FID < 30 (domain‑specific), Precision > 0.9, Recall > 0.85 | | **Radiomics match** | KS/EMD on ≥ 30 radiomic features. | KS p > 0.05, EMD < 0.02 | | **Expert blind test** | ≥ 3 readers, 200+ cases, AUC ≈ 0.5 for “real vs. fake”. | AUC 0.45–0.55, κ ≥ 0.8 | | **Down‑stream task** | Train with/without synthetic; non‑inferiority test. | ΔAUROC ≤ 0.03, ΔDice ≥ ‑0.01 | | **Privacy** | Membership‑inference attack success ≤ 55 %; DP ε ≤ 5 (if used). | | **Bias** | No statistically significant disparity across age/sex/ethnicity (χ² p > 0.05). | | **Robustness** | Performance unchanged (< 2 % loss) on out‑of‑distribution scanners. | | **Traceability** | Full Git/Docker provenance + data‑sheet + SOP. | | **Regulatory package** | SDVS + risk analysis + GMLP compliance checklist. | If **all** the above boxes are green, the synthetic medical images can be **considered validated** for: * **Data augmentation** in model training, * **Pre‑training** of downstream networks, * **Simulation / education** (e.g., teaching cases), and * **Limited clinical decision‑support** (after a formal SaMD clearance). question: How do precise measurements of rare B meson decays into muon pairs constrain extensions of the Standard Model, and which classes of new-physics models are most strongly affected by these results?
seed_answer:
**Short answer**

- **Why the decay matters** – The branching fraction \( \mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) (and the related \(B_{d}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)) is a *flavour‑changing neutral‑current* (FCNC) process that is forbidden at tree level in the Standard Model (SM) and can only occur through loop (penguin‑ and box‑) diagrams.  Its SM prediction is tiny (≈ \(3.66\times10^{-9}\) for \(B_{s}^{0}\) and ≈ \(1.06\times10^{-10}\) for \(B_{d}^{0}\)) and is known with a theoretical uncertainty of only ~ 5 % because the dominant hadronic input is the decay constant \(f_{B_{s,d}}\), which is now computed on the lattice to sub‑percent precision.

- **What a precise measurement does** – Any new heavy particle that couples to quarks and leptons can enter the same loops, or even generate a *tree‑level* contribution if the new interaction violates the SM gauge structure.  Because the SM amplitude is already so small, even a modest‑size new‑physics (NP) contribution can change the branching fraction by a *relative* amount of 10‑30 % or more, a shift that is now experimentally resolvable.  Consequently the measured value (currently \(\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) = (3.0\pm0.4)\times10^{-9}\), in excellent agreement with the SM) translates directly into *bounds* on the Wilson coefficients of the effective operators that describe NP at the scale \(\mu\simeq m_{b}\).

- **How the bounds are expressed** – In the low‑energy effective Hamiltonian for \(b\to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) one writes  

  \[
  \mathcal{H}_{\text{eff}} = -\frac{4G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}
  \Bigl[ C_{10}\, O_{10} + C_{S}\, O_{S} + C_{P}\, O_{P}
  + C_{10}^{\prime}\, O_{10}^{\prime}+ C_{S}^{\prime}\, O_{S}^{\prime}+ C_{P}^{\prime}\, O_{P}^{\prime}\Bigr] + \text{h.c.}
  \]

  where  

  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  O_{10} &= (\bar s\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}b)(\bar\ell\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\ell),\\
  O_{S}  &= m_{b}(\bar s P_{R}b)(\bar\ell\ell),\\
  O_{P}  &= m_{b}(\bar s P_{R}b)(\bar\ell\gamma_{5}\ell),
  \end{aligned}
  \]

  and the primed operators have opposite chirality (\(P_{L}\leftrightarrow P_{R}\)).  The SM contributes only to \(C_{10}^{\rm SM}\simeq -4.2\); the scalar/pseudoscalar coefficients are essentially zero.  The decay rate (ignoring tiny lepton‑mass terms for \(\mu\)) is

  \[
  \mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) =
  \frac{G_{F}^{2}\alpha^{2}}{16\pi^{3}}\,\tau_{B_s} f_{B_s}^{2} m_{B_s} m_{\mu}^{2}
  \sqrt{1-\frac{4m_{\mu}^{2}}{m_{B_s}^{2}}}\,
  \bigl|C_{10}^{\rm eff} + \frac{m_{B_s}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}}(C_{P} - C_{P}^{\prime})\bigr|^{2}
  + \frac{m_{B_s}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}^{2}}(C_{S} - C_{S}^{\prime})^{2},
  \]

  so any NP that generates non‑zero \(C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}\) or modifies \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) is directly constrained.

- **Resulting numerical limits** – Using the latest LHCb‑CMS combination (Run 1 + Run 2) together with the lattice average for \(f_{B_{s}}\), one finds at 95 % CL (schematic numbers, model‑independent):

  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  |C_{10}^{\rm NP}| &\lesssim 0.3,\\
  |C_{10}^{\prime}| &\lesssim 0.3,\\
  |C_{S,P}| &\lesssim 0.05,\quad |C_{S,P}^{\prime}| \lesssim 0.05,
  \end{aligned}
  \]

  where the SM value is \(C_{10}^{\rm SM}\approx -4.2\).  In other words, *any NP that contributes at the level of ∼ 10 % of the SM amplitude is already excluded*.

---

## Which classes of new‑physics models feel the pressure most?

| Model class | Typical effect on \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) | Why the bound is strong | Representative papers (post‑2022) |
|------------|-----------------------------------------------|--------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Supersymmetry with large \(\tan\beta\)** (MSSM, NMSSM) | Higgs‑mediated scalar/pseudoscalar operators \(C_{S,P}\propto (\tan\beta)^{3}/M_{A}^{2}\) | The amplitude grows like \(\tan^{3}\beta\); for \(\tan\beta\gtrsim 30\) even a heavy pseudoscalar \(M_{A}\sim 1\) TeV would overshoot the measured rate. | *Altmannshofer, Buras, et al.*, JHEP 2023 “\(B_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) in the MSSM after LHC Run‑2” |
| **Z′ models** (extra gauge boson coupling to \(b\)–\(s\) current) | Tree‑level contribution to \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) via \(Z′\) exchange | A vector boson with flavour‑changing coupling \(g_{bs}\) induces \(\Delta C_{10}\sim (g_{bs} g_{\mu\mu})/M_{Z′}^{2}\).  Current data require \(|g_{bs} g_{\mu\mu}|/M_{Z′}^{2}\lesssim 10^{-9}\,\text{GeV}^{-2}\), pushing the combination to either tiny couplings or \(M_{Z′}\gtrsim 5\) TeV for order‑one couplings. | *B‑physics constraints on Z′*, Phys. Rev. D 2024 |
| **Leptoquarks (LQ)** (scalar \(S_{3}\), vector \(U_{1}\), etc.) | Can affect both \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) and scalar/pseudoscalar coefficients depending on the LQ representation and chirality of couplings | Under the minimal flavour violation (MFV) hypothesis the same LQ that explains the \(R_{K^{(*)}}\) anomalies also generates a contribution to \(C_{10}^{\prime}\); the measured \(\mathcal{B}\) limits the product of quark–lepton couplings to \(|\lambda_{b\mu}\lambda_{s\mu}^{*}| \lesssim  (0.02)(M_{\text{LQ}}/\text{TeV})^{2}\). | *Dorsner, Greljo, et al.*, JHEP 2024 “Leptoquark fits after \(B_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)” |
| **Two‑Higgs‑Doublet Models (2HDM) of type II, X** | Same as SUSY Higgs‑mediated scalars (proportional to \(\tan^{2}\beta/M_{A}^{2}\)) | The alignment limit (SM‑like 125 GeV Higgs) does not suppress the flavour‑changing neutral Higgs coupling; therefore large \(\tan\beta\) is disfavoured unless the heavy Higgses are multi‑TeV. | *Crivellin, Heeck*, Eur. Phys. J. C 2023 |
| **Models with light (pseudo)‑scalar mediators** (axion‑like particles, dark photons with scalar mixing) | Can introduce a *resonant* enhancement if the mediator mass ≈ \(m_{B_{s}}\); otherwise they generate effective scalar operators. | The measured rate leaves little room for a new light particle that couples to \(\bar b s\) and \(\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\); limits on the effective coupling are \(\lesssim 10^{-5}\) for a 1‑GeV mediator. | *Kahn, Thaler* PRD 2022 “Constraints on light scalars from rare B decays”. |
| **Flavor‑changing neutral currents from compositeness / partial compositeness** | Generally give sizable contributions to \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) through exchange of composite vector resonances. | Electroweak precision forces the resonances heavy, but the \(\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) branching fraction pushes their effective scale to > 10 TeV, tightening the compositeness scale bound. | *Redi, Tesi*, JHEP 2023 |

### Bottom line for each class

| Model class | Dominant Wilson coefficient(s) affected | Approximate exclusion reach from \(\mathcal{B}(B_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) |
|-------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| SUSY at large \(\tan\beta\) | \(C_{S}, C_{P}\) (∝ \(\tan^{3}\beta/M_{A}^{2}\)) | \(\tan\beta \lesssim 30\) for \(M_{A}\lesssim 2\) TeV; otherwise heavy Higgs > 5 TeV |
| Generic Z′ | \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) (tree level) | \(|g_{bs} g_{\mu\mu}|/M_{Z′}^{2} \lesssim 10^{-9}\,\text{GeV}^{-2}\) → \(M_{Z′}\gtrsim 5\) TeV if couplings ≈ 1 |
| Leptoquarks | \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) and/or \(C_{S,P}\) | \(|\lambda_{b\mu}\lambda_{s\mu}^{*}| \lesssim 0.02 (M_{\text{LQ}}/\text{TeV})^{2}\) |
| 2HDM (type II/X) | \(C_{S,P}\) | \(\tan\beta/M_{A} \lesssim 0.03\) GeV\(^{-1}\) (so \(\tan\beta\sim 10\) forces \(M_{A} \gtrsim 300\) GeV) |
| Light scalar mediator | \(C_{S,P}\) (via off‑shell exchange) | Effective coupling \(y_{bs} y_{\mu\mu}\lesssim 10^{-5}\) for \(m_{\phi}\sim 1\) GeV |
| Composite‑Higgs / partial compositeness | \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}\) | Compositeness scale \(\Lambda \gtrsim 10\) TeV |

---

## How the experimental picture will improve

| Future milestone | Expected precision | Impact on NP reaches |
|------------------|--------------------|----------------------|
| **LHCb Upgrade I (Run 3, 2029)** | \(\delta\mathcal{B}/\mathcal{B}\approx 7\%\) (stat.) + systematic ≈ 5 % | Tighten the bound on scalar Wilson coeffs by ≈ 30 % → \(|C_{S,P}| \lesssim 0.03\). |
| **CMS‑Phase‑2 & ATLAS HL‑LHC** | Combined \(\sim\) 5 % total uncertainty | Push \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\) down to ≈ 0.15, i.e. ≈ 3 % of the SM amplitude. |
| **Belle II (full 50 ab\(^{-1}\))** | Similar percent‑level precision but with different systematics (e.g. no hadron‑trigger bias) | Provide an independent cross‑check; also measure the *effective lifetime* \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) which isolates the CP‑odd component and directly probes the relative phase of scalar vs. axial operators. |
| **Combined global fit (2026‑2028)** | \(\sigma(C_{i})\) ≈ 0.1 % of SM for \(C_{10}\); ≈ 0.01 for scalar coeffs | NP scales up to **≈ 30 TeV** for tree‑level Z′/LQ, **≈ 10 TeV** for loop‑induced SUSY‑type contributions, and **\(\tan\beta/M_{A}\) < 0.01 GeV\(^{-1}\)** for 2HDM‑type scalars. |

---

### Take‑away summary

1. **The decay \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) is a clean, theoretically pristine probe** – the SM prediction is precise, the experimental measurement is now at the 10‑% level, and the observable depends on a very limited set of effective operators.

2. **Precision data translate into tight bounds on the Wilson coefficients** \(C_{10}^{(\prime)}, C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}\).  Numerically, deviations larger than a few‑tenths of the SM value for \(C_{10}\) or larger than a few‑hundredths for scalar/pseudoscalar coefficients are excluded.

3. **Models that generate scalar/pseudoscalar operators are most constrained** – especially supersymmetric extensions with large \(\tan\beta\), generic two‑Higgs‑doublet models, and any light scalar mediator.  These typically receive an enhancement \(\propto \tan^{3}\beta\) or \(\propto 1/M_{A}^{2}\) and are forced into the decoupling regime (heavy Higgses, small \(\tan\beta\)).

4. **Tree‑level flavour‑changing vector mediators (Z′, leptoquarks) are also squeezed**, but the bound is *model‑dependent*: it limits the product of quark and lepton couplings divided by the squared mass.  For order‑unity couplings the new boson must be heavier than ~5 TeV.

5. **Future upgrades will sharpen the picture** – by the end of the HL‑LHC era the allowed NP contribution to the branching fraction will be at the few‑percent level, pushing the effective NP scale for tree‑level mediators well beyond 10 TeV and forcing loop‑induced models to be highly suppressed or highly aligned with the SM flavour structure.

In short, the *precise* measurement of rare \(B\)-meson decays into muon pairs is now one of the most powerful indirect probes of physics beyond the Standard Model, and it currently places the strongest constraints on any theory that predicts sizable scalar/pseudoscalar couplings or tree‑level flavour‑changing neutral currents.

question: How can measurements of very rare neutral meson decays into lepton pairs be used to test the Standard Model and constrain theories of physics beyond the Standard Model?
seed_answer:
## Overview  

Rare decays of neutral mesons ( \(P^0 = K_L,\;K_S,\;D^0,\;B^0,\;B_s^0,\;B_d^0,\;\pi^0,\;\eta,\;\eta',\;J/\psi,\;\Upsilon\) ) into a pair of charged leptons ( \(e^+e^-\), \(\mu^+\mu^-\), \(\tau^+\tau^-\) ) occupy a privileged position in flavor‑physics.  

* They are **flavor‑changing neutral currents** (FCNC) or, for truly neutral mesons, **Lepton‑Flavor–Conserving** but **loop‑suppressed** processes.  
* In the Standard Model (SM) they occur only through higher‑order electroweak diagrams (penguins, box diagrams) and are further damped by the **Glashow‑Iliopoulos‑Maiani (GIM) mechanism** and, in many cases, by **helicity suppression** \(\propto m_\ell^2\).  
* Consequently the SM branching fractions are tiny (10⁻⁶–10⁻¹⁰ or smaller), often comparable to the experimental sensitivity of modern detectors.  

Any **deviation** from the SM prediction—either an unexpected rate, an anomalous angular distribution, or a lepton‑flavor‑violating (LFV) signal—must arise from **new particles or interactions** that either (i) enter the loop, (ii) generate a tree‑level contribution, or (iii) modify the effective operators that describe the decay at low energy.

Below we detail how precision measurements (or stringent upper limits) of these processes are turned into **tests of the SM** and **constraints on physics beyond the SM (BSM)**.

---

## 1. Theoretical framework  

### 1.1 Effective Hamiltonian for \(P^0\to \ell^+\ell^-\)

At scales \(\mu\sim m_b, m_c, m_s\) the short‑distance dynamics of FCNC decays are captured by an **effective weak Hamiltonian**  

\[
\mathcal{H}_{\rm eff}= -\frac{G_F}{\sqrt2}\,\frac{\alpha}{2\pi s_W^2}\,V_{tb}^{(\ast)}V_{tq}\,\sum_i C_i(\mu) \,Q_i(\mu) + \text{h.c.},
\]

where  

* \(q = d, s, c\) for \(B_{d,s}, K, D\) decays,  
* \(Q_i\) are dimension‑six operators (vector, axial‑vector, scalar, pseudoscalar, electromagnetic dipole),  
* \(C_i\) are Wilson coefficients encoding short‑distance physics (SM loops plus possible BSM contributions).  

The **relevant operators** for a purely leptonic final state are  

| Operator | Definition | SM source |
|----------|------------|-----------|
|\(Q_{10}\) | \((\bar q \gamma_\mu P_L b)(\bar\ell \gamma^\mu\gamma_5 \ell)\) | Z‑penguin & box |
|\(Q_{S}\)   | \((\bar q P_R b)(\bar\ell \ell)\) | Higgs‑penguin (tiny) |
|\(Q_{P}\)   | \((\bar q P_R b)(\bar\ell \gamma_5 \ell)\) | Pseudoscalar Higgs (tiny) |
|\(Q_{7\gamma}\) | \((\bar q \sigma_{\mu\nu} P_R b)F^{\mu\nu}\) | Radiative penguin (feeds via virtual photon) |

The **branching ratio** for a neutral meson \(P^0\) of mass \(M\) decaying to \(\ell^+\ell^-\) can be written (to a very good approximation) as  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{B}(P^0\!\to\!\ell^+\ell^-) &=
\frac{G_F^2\alpha^2}{16\pi^3}\,M\,\tau_{P}\,f_{P}^2
\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_\ell^2}{M^2}}\\
&\times \Bigl|
C_{10}^{\rm eff}\, \frac{2m_\ell}{M}+C_{P}^{\rm eff}\frac{M}{m_b+m_q}
+ C_{S}^{\rm eff}\frac{M}{m_b+m_q}\Bigr|^{\!2},
\end{aligned}
}
\]

where  

* \(f_P\) is the decay constant (obtained from lattice QCD),  
* \(C_{10}^{\rm eff}=C_{10}+Y(q^2)\) includes the perturbative “\(Y\)” function from the virtual photon,  
* \(C_{S,P}^{\rm eff}\) vanish in the SM (except for higher‑order Higgs‑penguins), so any sizable contribution signals BSM physics.

**Key points**  

* **Helicity suppression**: the term proportional to \(C_{10}^{\rm eff}\) carries a factor \(m_\ell\). Hence decays to electrons are far rarer than to muons or taus.  
* **Scalar/pseudoscalar operators** lift the helicity suppression – they are a smoking gun for BSM (e.g. supersymmetric Higgs, leptoquarks, Z′ with scalar couplings).  

---

### 1.2 Connecting to specific BSM models  

| BSM scenario | Typical effect on \(C_i\) | Observable impact |
|--------------|---------------------------|-------------------|
| **Minimal Supersymmetric SM (MSSM) at large \(\tan\beta\)** | Enhances \(C_S, C_P\) ∝ \(\tan^3\beta / M_A^2\) (Higgs‑mediated) | \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)\) can be *order‑of‑magnitude* larger; strong lepton‑mass scaling. |
| **Z′ boson with flavor‑changing couplings** | Shifts \(C_{10}\) (vector/axial) and can introduce right‑handed operators \(Q_{10}′\) | Modifies angular observables in semileptonic decays, changes rate of \(K_L\to\mu^+\mu^-\). |
| **Leptoquarks** | Generate scalar/pseudoscalar and/or tensor operators at tree level | May produce observable \(B_{(d,s)}\to e^\pm\mu^\mp\) (LFV) and alter \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\tau^+\tau^-)\). |
| **Dark photons / light hidden scalars** | Appear as on‑shell intermediate states \(P^0\to \gamma A′, A′\to \ell^+\ell^-\) | Produce a *bump* in the dilepton invariant‑mass spectrum inside the otherwise two‑body decay. |
| **Composite Higgs / partial compositeness** | Modify the Z‑penguin, shifting \(C_{10}\) and generating right‑handed currents | Small, correlated deviations across \(K\), \(B_d\), and \(B_s\) decay rates. |

The **experimental observable** linked to a given Wilson coefficient is not only the total branching ratio but also—when enough events are collected—kinematic distributions (e.g. time‑dependent CP asymmetry in \(K_L\) decays, forward–backward asymmetry in \(B\to K^{(*)}\ell^+\ell^-\) but also in the pure leptonic case the **effective lifetime**).  

---

## 2. Experimental landscape  

| Decay | SM BR (approx.) | Current best measurement / limit | Main experiments |
|-------|----------------|-----------------------------------|-------------------|
| \(K_L \to \mu^+\mu^-\) | \(\sim 7\times10^{-9}\) (long‑distance dominated) | \((6.84\pm0.11)\times10^{-9}\) (NA62) | NA62, KOTO |
| \(K_S \to \mu^+\mu^-\) | \(\sim 5\times10^{-12}\) | \(< 1.0\times10^{-9}\) (LHCb) | LHCb, future Kaon factories |
| \(\pi^0 \to e^+e^-\) | \(\sim 7\times10^{-8}\) | \((7.48\pm0.29)\times10^{-8}\) (KTeV) | KTeV, future NA62/REDTOP |
| \(\eta \to \mu^+\mu^-\) | \(\sim 5\times10^{-6}\) | \((5.8\pm0.8)\times10^{-6}\) (PDG) | BESIII, future REDTOP |
| \(B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-\) | \((3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9}\) | \((3.0\pm0.4)\times10^{-9}\) (LHCb+CMS) | LHCb, CMS, ATLAS, future HL‑LHC |
| \(B_d \to \mu^+\mu^-\) | \((1.06\pm0.04)\times10^{-10}\) | \((1.0\pm0.3)\times10^{-10}\) (LHCb) | LHCb, HL‑LHC |
| \(D^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-\) | \(\sim 10^{-13}\) (long‑distance) | \(< 6.2\times10^{-9}\) (LHCb) | LHCb, Belle II |
| \(J/\psi \to e^+e^-,\;\mu^+\mu^-\) | \(\sim 6\%\) (EM) – not FCNC, but **LFV** modes are forbidden | \(< 10^{-7}\) for \(J/\psi\to e^\pm\mu^\mp\) | BESIII |
| \(\Upsilon(1S,2S,3S) \to \ell^+\ell^-\) | \(\sim\) few % (EM) – LFV limits at <10⁻⁶ | — | Belle II, BaBar |

*The numbers are indicative; the values evolve with each data release.*

### 2.1 What experiments actually measure  

1. **Branching ratios** (or upper limits) – direct comparison with the SM prediction.  
2. **Effective lifetimes** (especially for \(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-\)) – the SM predicts a specific mixture of CP‑even and CP‑odd states; new scalar operators alter the decay‑width difference \(\Delta\Gamma_s\).  
3. **Time‑dependent CP asymmetries** in kaon decays (e.g. \(K_L\to\mu^+\mu^-\) vs \(K_S\to\mu^+\mu^-\)).  
4. **Lepton‑flavor-violating modes** (e.g. \(K_L\to e^\pm\mu^\mp\), \(B^0\to e^\pm\mu^\mp\)) – any observation is a clean BSM signal because the SM rate is strictly zero (up to neutrino‑mixing‑suppressed contributions ≪10⁻⁵⁰).  
5. **Invariant‑mass spectra** for processes where an intermediate light boson could appear, e.g. \(B\to K A′\), \(A′\to\ell^+\ell^-\).  

---

## 3. From measurement to SM test  

### 3.1 Computing the SM prediction  

* **Short‑distance part** – calculated to next‑to‑next‑to‑leading order (NNLO) in QCD/EW for \(B_{s,d}\) decays; includes two‑loop electroweak boxes, three‑loop QCD anomalous dimensions.  
* **Long‑distance contributions** – especially important for kaons and pions: the decay proceeds via \(P^0\to\gamma\gamma\) with the photons converting to \(\ell^+\ell^-\). Dispersion‑relation techniques, chiral perturbation theory, and lattice QCD are used to estimate the “absorptive” part (dominant for \(K_L\to\mu^+\mu^-\)).  
* **Hadronic inputs** – decay constants \(f_{P}\), bag parameters, and form factors are supplied by lattice QCD with sub‑percent uncertainties for \(B_{s,d}\) and a few‑percent for kaons.  

The **theoretical uncertainty budget** is now at the **few‑percent level** for \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^+\mu^-\) and at the **10‑20 % level** for \(K_L\to\mu^+\mu^-\) (where the long‑distance piece dominates).  

### 3.2 Consistency checks  

* **Branching‑ratio consistency** – the measured \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-)\) agrees with the SM within ≈ 1 σ. This already **excludes** large scalar contributions such as those predicted by MSSM with \(\tan\beta\gtrsim 50\) and \(M_A\lesssim 500\) GeV.  
* **Correlation with other FCNC observables** – Global fits (e.g. using *flavio*, *EOS*, *HEPfit*) incorporate \(b\to s\ell^+\ell^-\) angular observables, \(B\to K^{(*)}\nu\bar\nu\), and \(\Delta M_{s,d}\). The current best‑fit point is very close to the SM, leaving only modest room for BSM shifts in \(C_{10}\) (\(|\Delta C_{10}|\lesssim 0.2\)).  
* **Effective lifetime** – LHCb's measurement of \(\tau_{\mu\mu}^{B_s}=1.70\pm0.04\) ps is consistent with the SM expectation (1.61 ps). Any sizable scalar contribution would increase the CP‑even fraction and **shorten** the lifetime, so the data already *constrain* \(|C_S|,|C_P|\lesssim 0.1\) (in SM‑normalized units).  

---

## 4. Translating limits into BSM constraints  

Below we illustrate the procedure for two emblematic cases.

### 4.1 Example 1: MSSM Higgs‑mediated scalar operators  

In the large‑\(\tan\beta\) regime, the dominant BSM contribution to \(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-\) reads  

\[
C_{S}^{\rm MSSM} \simeq -\,\frac{m_b m_\mu \,\tan^3\beta}{4 M_A^{2}}\,
\frac{(\mu A_t)}{M_{\rm SUSY}^{2}}\,\frac{16\pi^2}{\alpha\,Y_0(x_t)},
\]

where \(M_A\) is the CP‑odd Higgs mass, \(\mu\) the higgsino mass parameter, \(A_t\) the stop trilinear coupling, and \(M_{\rm SUSY}\) a common superpartner mass scale.  

Using the measured branching ratio  

\[
\mathcal{B}^{\rm exp}(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-) = (3.0\pm0.4)\times10^{-9},
\]

and the SM prediction \(\mathcal{B}^{\rm SM}= (3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9}\), one obtains a **95 % C.L. bound** on the scalar contribution  

\[
|C_S| \lesssim 0.07.
\]

Plugging the expression for \(C_S\) and assuming a typical SUSY spectrum (\(\mu, A_t, M_{\rm SUSY}\sim 1\) TeV) yields  

\[
M_A \gtrsim 1.2\;\text{TeV}\times\left(\frac{\tan\beta}{50}\right)^{3/2}.
\]

Thus **current data already push the heavy Higgs mass well above the direct‑search limit** for large \(\tan\beta\).

### 4.2 Example 2: Leptoquark‑induced LFV decay \(K_L \to e^\pm\mu^\mp\)

A vector leptoquark \(U_1\) coupling to left‑handed quarks and leptons generates at tree level the operator  

\[
\mathcal{O}_{\rm LFV}= (\bar s \gamma_\mu d)(\bar e \gamma^\mu \mu),
\]

with Wilson coefficient  

\[
C_{\rm LFV}= \frac{g_U^2}{2M_U^2}\, (V_{U})_{s e}(V_U^\dagger)_{\mu d}.
\]

The branching ratio is  

\[
\mathcal{B}(K_L\to e^\pm\mu^\mp)=\frac{\tau_{K_L}}{16\pi M_{K}}\,
f_K^{2}\,|C_{\rm LFV}|^{2}\,M_{K}^{2}\sqrt{1-\frac{(m_e+m_\mu)^2}{M_K^2}}.
\]

The **experimental upper limit** from KOTO/NA62 is  

\[
\mathcal{B}(K_L\to e^\pm\mu^\mp) < 4.7\times10^{-12}\;(90\%\,\text{C.L.}).
\]

Translating this into a bound on the leptoquark parameters (taking \(g_U=1\)) gives  

\[
\frac{|(V_{U})_{s e}(V_U^\dagger)_{\mu d}|}{M_U^{2}} \lesssim 3\times10^{-13}\;\text{GeV}^{-2},
\]

or, for order‑one flavor couplings, **\(M_U \gtrsim 1.8\) PeV**. This demonstrates that **rare LFV meson decays probe energy scales far beyond the direct reach of colliders**.

---

## 5. Complementarity with other probes  

| Probe | Typical scale reached | Unique information |
|-------|-----------------------|--------------------|
| **\(B_{s,d}\to\mu^+\mu^-\)** | \(\sim\)10 TeV (scalar) / 5 TeV (vector) | Direct test of scalar–pseudoscalar operators, probes CP properties via effective lifetime. |
| **\(K\to\pi\nu\bar\nu\)** | \(\sim\)50 TeV | Sensitive to Z‑penguin and box, but with neutrinos → complementary flavor structure. |
| **\(b\to s\ell^+\ell^-\) angular observables** | \(\sim\)10 TeV | Mainly vector/axial operators, provide information on right‑handed currents. |
| **LFV decays (e.g. \(\mu\to e\gamma\), \(\tau\to\mu\gamma\))** | \(\sim\)100 TeV | Direct probes of lepton‑flavor violation, independent of quark flavor. |
| **High‑\(p_T\) Drell‑Yan at the LHC** | \(\sim\)5–6 TeV | Constraints on contact interactions; less sensitive to helicity‑suppressed scalar operators. |

Thus, a **global analysis** that includes all rare‑decay channels, LFV limits, and high‑energy collider data maximises the reach and can **disentangle the operator structure** of any new physics that may finally show up.

---

## 6. Outlook – Future improvements  

| Decay | Expected sensitivity (HL‑LHC / Belle II / dedicated Kaon experiments) | Impact |
|------|--------------------------------------------|--------|
| \(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-\) (branching & lifetime) | \(\sim 5\%\) on BR, \(\pm0.02\) ps on lifetime | Shrink scalar‑operator window to \(|C_S| \lesssim 0.02\). |
| \(B_d\to\mu^+\mu^-\) | reach \(< 5\times10^{-11}\) | Test SM ratio \(\mathcal{B}(B_d)/\mathcal{B}(B_s)\) (flavor‑universality). |
| \(K_L\to\mu^+\mu^-\) (short‑distance component) | 10 % precision via improved theory + data | Separate long‑ and short‑distance parts, directly constrain \(C_{10}\) in the kaon sector. |
| \(K_L\to e^\pm\mu^\mp\) | \(\mathcal{O}(10^{-13})\) upper limit (KOTO‑II) | Push LFV scale beyond 10 PeV for order‑one couplings. |
| \(\pi^0,\eta\to e^+e^-\) | 5 % precision (REDTOP) | Test ChPT and dispersion calculations; any excess hints at light dark mediators. |
| \(\Upsilon\to \ell^+\ell^-\) (LFV) | \(<10^{-7}\) (Belle II) | Complementary probe of leptoquarks coupling to the third generation. |

The **theoretical community** is also advancing:  

* **Lattice QCD** will deliver sub‑percent decay constants for \(K\) and \(D\) mesons, and continue reducing uncertainties for \(B_{s,d}\).  
* **Dispersive analyses** of the long‑distance part of \(K_L\to\mu^+\mu^-\) are being refined, which will allow a clean extraction of the short‑distance piece.  
* **Automated global EFT fits** (e.g. *smelli*, *flavio*) will incorporate forthcoming results in real time, delivering up‑to‑date limits on Wilson coefficients.  

---

## 7. Take‑home messages  

1. **Rare neutral‑meson decays to lepton pairs are loop‑suppressed, helicity‑suppressed, and often GIM‑suppressed in the SM**, leading to tiny but precisely calculable branching fractions.  

2. **Any deviation—whether an excess rate, a different effective lifetime, or a lepton‑flavor‑violating signature—directly maps onto changes in the Wilson coefficients \(C_{10}, C_S, C_P\) (or their primed counterparts)** of the low‑energy effective Hamiltonian.  

3. Present measurements of \(B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-\) already **exclude large scalar contributions** from models such as high‑\(\tan\beta\) MSSM, pushing the relevant new‑physics scale to the multi‑TeV regime.  

4. **Upper limits on LFV modes** such as \(K_L\to e^\pm\mu^\mp\) reach **effective scales of 10 PeV**, far beyond any direct collider.  

5. **Future experiments** (HL‑LHC, Belle II, NA62/KOTO‑II, REDTOP) will shrink experimental uncertainties to the few‑percent level, turning these decays into *precision* probes of the SM and *high‑sensitivity* windows onto BSM physics.  

6. The **full power** of these tests emerges only in a **global EFT fit**, where the pattern of (non‑)deviations across kaon, charm, and beauty sectors, together with LFV and high‑\(p_T\) data, can pinpoint the flavor structure, chiral nature, and mass scale of any new interaction.  

In short, **very rare neutral‑meson leptonic decays are among the cleanest and most incisive laboratories for testing the Standard Model and for reaching toward the deepest layers of physics beyond it.**

question: How do precise measurements of rare neutral B meson decays into muon pairs constrain theories beyond the Standard Model, and why are these particular decays so sensitive to new physics?

### 1.
